sessions.title: What Are Living Things?
indicators: Identify living things in the immediate environment
State the characteristics of living things (they grow, breathe, eat, move, reproduce)
Distinguish between living and non-living things by observing pictures and objects
Work in pairs to sort pictures into living and non-living groups (collaboration)
Use digital slideshows or videos to explore living things (digital literacy)
Appreciate that all living things need care and respect (personal development)
sessions.content:
Living Things Around Us

Everything around us can be put into two groups: living things and non-living things. Living things are alive. They grow, breathe, eat, move and have young ones.

1. Characteristics of Living Things

Living things do these things:

  • Grow: A baby chick grows into a hen. A small mango seed grows into a big tree.
  • Breathe: We take in air. Fish breathe in water.
  • Eat: A goat eats grass. We eat kenkey, rice, fruits.
  • Move: A bird flies. A snake crawls. A child runs.
  • Reproduce (have young ones): A dog gives birth to puppies. A hen lays eggs that hatch into chicks.

Examples of living things: boy, girl, cat, mango tree, maize plant, fish, butterfly, teacher, ant.

Activity 1 – Living things hunt
Walk around the school garden or look out the window. Point to five living things. Say their names and one thing each can do: The bird flies. The grass grows. (collaboration).

2. Non-Living Things

Non-living things are not alive. They do not grow, eat, breathe, move on their own, or have young ones.

Examples: stone, pencil, desk, water, car, book, chair, ball.

Activity 2 – Picture sort
In pairs, sort a set of picture cards into two hoops: Living and Non-Living. Explain why you placed each item. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Watch a short animated video on a tablet about living and non-living things. Pause after each example and say if it is living or non-living. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.1

  1. Name three living things in your classroom.
  2. Name two non-living things you can see outside.
  3. Write one thing that a living thing can do that a non-living thing cannot.
  4. Draw a living thing and a non-living thing. Label them.

sessions.title: Differences Between Living and Non-Living Things
indicators: Compare a living thing with a non-living thing using a checklist
Explain why something is non-living (e.g., does not eat or grow)
Observe and record differences between a real plant and a toy plant
Work in small groups to create a comparison chart (collaboration)
Use an interactive digital quiz to test knowledge (digital literacy)
Develop curiosity about the natural world (personal development)
sessions.content:
Alive or Not? – How to Tell

To decide if something is living, we can ask five questions: Does it grow? Does it breathe? Does it eat? Does it move by itself? Can it have young ones? If the answer is yes to most, it is living. If not, it is non-living.

1. Checklist for Living Things

Use this checklist. Put a tick (✓) or cross (✗).

QuestionCatStone
Does it grow?✓✗
Does it breathe?✓✗
Does it eat?✓✗
Does it move by itself?✓✗
Can it have young ones?✓✗

The cat is living. The stone is non-living.

Activity 1 – Compare a plant and a toy plant
Observe a real potted plant and a plastic plant. Touch and look at both. Discuss: Does the real plant grow? Does the toy plant grow? Does the real plant need water? Fill in a checklist together. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Living or non-living quiz
Teacher says a word: bicycle, fish, book, tree, baby, sand. Pupils stand up if it is living and sit down if it is non-living. (communication).

Digital corner: Use a simple online quiz (e.g., on a tablet) where pupils tap Living or Non-Living for each picture. The app gives instant feedback. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.2

  1. Use the checklist to decide if a butterfly is living. Write yes for each question.
  2. Why is water not a living thing? Give two reasons.
  3. Draw a toy car and a real dog. Label them living and non-living.
  4. Name one thing that was once living but is now non-living (e.g., a wooden chair).

sessions.title: Parts of a Plant
indicators: Identify the main parts of a plant: roots, stem, leaves, flower, fruit
Describe the function of each part in simple terms
Observe real plants and label the parts
Work in groups to draw and label a plant (collaboration)
Use digital resources to explore plant parts (digital literacy)
Appreciate that plants give us food, medicine and shade (personal development)
sessions.content:
Know Your Plant – Roots to Leaves

Plants are living things. Most plants have five main parts. Each part has a job.

1. Plant Parts and Their Jobs

  • Roots: Hold the plant firmly in the ground. They also suck water and nutrients from the soil. Example: carrot, cassava (we eat some roots).
  • Stem: Supports the plant and holds up leaves, flowers and fruits. It carries water from roots to leaves. Example: sugar cane stem, plantain stem.
  • Leaves: Make food for the plant using sunlight. They are like the plant's kitchen. Example: cocoyam leaf, mango leaf.
  • Flower: Makes seeds and fruits. It is often colourful to attract insects. Example: hibiscus flower, rose.
  • Fruit: Protects the seeds and helps them spread. We eat many fruits. Example: orange, mango, tomato, pepper.

Activity 1 – Pull and observe
Gently pull out a small weed or grass. Wash the roots. Observe the different parts. Point and name: roots, stem, leaves. If there is a flower or fruit, name them too. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Label a plant diagram
In groups, draw a large plant on a chart. Label the five parts. Use arrows to point. Display in class. (creativity, collaboration).

Digital corner: Use an interactive plant labelling app where you drag the names to the correct part. Hear the name spoken aloud. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.1

  1. Draw a plant. Label the roots, stem and leaves.
  2. Which part of the plant holds it in the soil? Write the answer.
  3. Name two fruits we eat that come from plants.
  4. What job do the leaves do? Explain in one sentence.

sessions.title: What Plants Need to Grow
indicators: Identify the four basic needs of plants: water, sunlight, air, soil (nutrients)
Describe what happens if a plant lacks one of these needs
Conduct a simple experiment growing seeds with and without water or light
Work in groups to care for a class plant (collaboration, personal development)
Record observations using digital photos or a class blog (digital literacy)
Develop responsibility by caring for a living thing (personal development)
sessions.content:
Help the Plant Grow – What Plants Need

Like all living things, plants need certain things to stay alive and grow. They need water, sunlight, air and soil.

1. The Four Needs

  • Water: Plants drink water through their roots. Without water, they wilt and dry out.
  • Sunlight: Plants use sunlight to make their food. A plant kept in a dark cupboard turns yellow.
  • Air: Plants breathe too! They take in air through tiny holes in their leaves.
  • Soil (nutrients): Soil gives plants minerals that act like vitamins. Good soil helps plants grow strong.

Example: If you water a potted plant and put it by the window, it grows green and healthy. If you forget to water it and keep it in a dark room, it becomes weak and may die.

Activity 1 – Seed growing experiment
Plant three bean seeds in three cups with soil. Cup A: give water and sunlight. Cup B: give water but keep in a dark box. Cup C: give sunlight but no water. Observe every day for one week. Draw what you see. (collaboration, critical thinking).

Activity 2 – Class plant care
As a class, decide on one plant to care for (e.g., a maize plant in a tin). Make a watering and sunlight rota. Pupils take turns to water and move the plant into the sun. (collaboration, personal development).

Digital corner: Take a photo of the plant every day with a tablet. Put the photos in order to make a time-lapse of growth. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.2

  1. Name the four things a plant needs to grow.
  2. What will happen to a plant that gets no water? Write one sentence.
  3. If you put a plant in a dark room, why does it turn yellow?
  4. Draw the experiment with three cups. Write what happened to each plant after one week.

sessions.title: Animals in the Environment
indicators: Name common domestic and wild animals found in Ghana
Group animals according to where they live (land, water, air)
Identify animals by the sounds they make
Work in groups to create an animal sound game (collaboration, creativity)
Use digital animal encyclopedias or apps to learn about animals (digital literacy)
Appreciate the need to protect animals and their homes (personal development)
sessions.content:
Animals All Around Us

Animals are living things. They can be found on land, in water, and some can fly in the air. Ghana has many different animals.

1. Animal Groups by Where They Live

  • Land animals: dog, goat, cat, cow, lion, elephant, snake, ant, lizard.
  • Water animals (aquatic): fish, crab, tilapia, crocodile, octopus.
  • Air animals (that fly): eagle, parrot, bat (it flies), butterfly, housefly.

Examples of animal sounds: Cat: meow. Dog: woof-woof. Cow: moo. Sheep: baa. Bird: chirp-chirp. Lion: roar. Frog: croak.

Activity 1 – Animal sound orchestra
Divide the class into groups: dogs, cats, birds, frogs. Teacher points to a group, they make their animal sound. Point to all: a chorus of sounds! (creativity, collaboration).

Activity 2 – Where do I live?
Show pictures of animals. Pupils place them in three circles drawn on the floor labelled Land, Water, Air. Discuss: Why can’t a fish live on land? (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a child-friendly animal app to listen to the sound an animal makes, see where it lives, and watch a short video. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.1

  1. Name two animals that live on land and two that live in water.
  2. What sound does a sheep make? Write it.
  3. Draw a fish and write one sentence about why it lives in water.
  4. Why is it important to protect animals and their homes? Give one reason.

sessions.title: What Animals Eat
indicators: Identify animals that eat plants (herbivores), meat (carnivores) and both (omnivores) in simple terms
Group animals by what they eat
Explain why different animals need different food
Work in pairs to sort animal picture cards by their food (collaboration)
Use digital sorting games to classify animals by diet (digital literacy)
Recognise that all animals need food to survive (personal development)
sessions.content:
What’s for Dinner? – Animal Diets

Animals eat different kinds of food. Some eat only plants. Some eat only other animals. Some eat both plants and animals.

1. Types of Eaters

  • Herbivores (plant-eaters): goat (grass), cow (grass), rabbit (carrots, leaves), grasshopper (leaves).
  • Carnivores (meat-eaters): lion (meat), cat (rats, fish), eagle (snakes, small birds), dog (meat, bones).
  • Omnivores (eat both): hen (grains and insects), pig (anything), human (rice, meat, fish).

Example: A goat eats grass only – it is a herbivore. A lion eats zebra meat – it is a carnivore. A chicken eats maize and worms – it is an omnivore.

Activity 1 – Food sorting
In pairs, get picture cards of animals and picture cards of food items. Match each animal to what it eats. Discuss why a cow cannot eat meat. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Guess the eater
Teacher describes an animal's diet: I eat only grass. Who am I? Pupils guess: goat, cow. I eat only meat. Who am I? Lion. I eat grains and small insects. Who am I? Chicken. (communication).

Digital corner: Use a sorting app where animals appear on screen and children drag them into the correct box: Plant-eater, Meat-eater, or Both. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.2

  1. Write whether each animal is a plant-eater, meat-eater or both: cow, dog, eagle, man.
  2. Why can't a goat eat fish? Explain in one sentence.
  3. Name one animal that eats both plants and animals.
  4. Draw a food chain: grass -> goat -> lion. Label who eats whom.

sessions.title: External Parts of the Body
indicators: Name and point to major external body parts: head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, neck, arms, hands, legs, feet
State the function of each body part in simple terms
Participate in action songs and games that identify body parts
Work in pairs to draw and label a body outline (collaboration)
Use interactive body labelling apps to reinforce learning (digital literacy)
Appreciate the need to keep all body parts clean (personal development)
sessions.content:
My Wonderful Body – Parts You Can See

Our body has many parts. Each part has a special job. We can see these parts on the outside. We must take care of them.

1. Body Parts and Their Functions

  • Head: contains the brain, which helps us think.
  • Eyes: for seeing. We have two eyes.
  • Ears: for hearing sounds.
  • Nose: for breathing and smelling.
  • Mouth: for eating, talking, smiling.
  • Neck: connects the head to the rest of the body.
  • Arms and hands: for holding, writing, carrying things.
  • Legs and feet: for standing, walking, running, jumping.

Activity 1 – Head, shoulders, knees and toes
Sing the action song: Head, shoulders, knees and toes, knees and toes... Touch each part as you sing. Gradually increase the speed. (creativity).

Activity 2 – Body tracing
In pairs, one pupil lies on a large sheet of paper while the other traces their body outline. Then both label as many parts as they can. (collaboration, creativity).

Digital corner: Use a body labelling app that speaks the name of the part when touched. Drag the label to the correct spot. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.1

  1. Draw a picture of yourself. Label your head, eyes, nose, mouth, arms and legs.
  2. What do you use your ears for? Write one sentence.
  3. Which body part helps you kick a ball?
  4. Why must we wash our hands? Give one reason.

sessions.title: Keeping Healthy – Cleanliness, Food and Exercise
indicators: Explain why we must wash our hands, bathe, brush teeth and keep our environment clean
Identify healthy foods (fruits, vegetables) and junk foods (sweets, chips) in simple terms
State the importance of exercise and sleep for a healthy body
Work in groups to create a healthy habits chart (collaboration)
Use digital tools to record personal hygiene routines (digital literacy)
Develop personal responsibility for health and cleanliness (personal development)
sessions.content:
Stay Strong and Healthy

To keep our body working well, we must keep clean, eat good food, exercise and rest.

1. Cleanliness (Hygiene)

  • Wash hands with soap and water before eating, after using the toilet, and after playing. This removes germs that make us sick.
  • Bathe every day to keep skin clean.
  • Brush teeth twice a day (morning and night) to prevent tooth decay.
  • Keep the environment clean: sweep the classroom, pick up litter, use the dustbin.

Example: After playing football, Kofi washes his hands with soap before eating his kenkey. This stops him from getting stomach ache.

2. Healthy Eating

Eat a variety of foods: fruits (orange, banana, pawpaw), vegetables (kontomire, garden eggs, tomatoes), grains (rice, maize), proteins (fish, beans, eggs). Limit sweets, biscuits and sugary drinks. Drink plenty of clean water.

Activity 1 – Sort the food
Show pictures of foods. In pairs, sort into two groups: Healthy foods and Sometimes foods (not so healthy). Discuss why fruits and vegetables are healthy. (collaboration).

3. Exercise and Sleep

Play and exercise every day (running, jumping, ampe). Exercise makes the heart and muscles strong. Sleep early and get enough rest (about 9-10 hours for children) so the body can repair and grow.

Activity 2 – Healthy habits chart
In groups, make a weekly chart with these daily tasks: I washed my hands before eating, I brushed my teeth, I exercised, I slept early. Tick each day you complete the task. (collaboration, personal development).

Digital corner: Use a simple habit-tracking app for kids to check off healthy habits. Or take a photo of your healthy meal and share with the class. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.2

  1. Write three times you should wash your hands.
  2. Name two healthy foods and one food you should eat less often.
  3. Why is exercise good for your body? Write one reason.
  4. Draw a bedtime routine that includes brushing teeth and sleeping early.

sessions.title: Types of Weather
indicators: Describe different types of weather: sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy
Identify the type of weather for the day
Relate weather to appropriate clothing and activities
Work in groups to make a weather chart for the week (collaboration)
Use digital weather apps or videos to observe weather patterns (digital literacy)
Appreciate how weather affects our daily lives (personal development)
sessions.content:
Look at the Sky – Weather

Weather is what the sky and air outside are like. It can change from day to day, even within a day.

1. Types of Weather

  • Sunny: The sun shines brightly. The sky is clear or has a few white clouds. We wear light clothing, hats. Good for playing outside.
  • Rainy: Water falls from clouds. We see dark clouds (nimbus). We carry umbrellas or raincoats, wear boots. Stay indoors if heavy rain with thunder and lightning.
  • Windy: The air moves strongly. Trees bend, leaves fly, dust rises. We hold our hats.
  • Cloudy: The sky is covered with grey or white clouds. It may not rain but looks dull.

Example: This morning it is sunny and hot. The weather reporter says this afternoon may be rainy with thunder. We carry an umbrella to school.

Activity 1 – Weather window
Look outside the window. Describe today's weather: Is it sunny? Rainy? Windy? Cloudy? Draw a picture of what you see and label it. (creativity).

Activity 2 – Weather chart
In groups, create a weekly weather chart. Each day, a pupil draws the weather symbol (sun for sunny, cloud and rain drops for rainy). At the end of the week, count how many sunny days and rainy days. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a tablet to check a simple weather forecast for the week. Compare with your own observations. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.1

  1. Draw the symbol for sunny weather and for rainy weather.
  2. What type of weather makes trees bend? Write the word.
  3. Why do we need an umbrella on a rainy day? Explain.
  4. Name one activity you do on a sunny day and one you do on a rainy day.

sessions.title: Water – Uses and Sources
indicators: Identify sources of water: rain, well, river, tap, borehole
List everyday uses of water: drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, farming
Explain why we must drink clean water and keep water sources clean
Work in pairs to make a poster on uses of water (creativity, collaboration)
Watch digital videos on water use and conservation (digital literacy)
Develop a sense of responsibility for saving water (personal development)
sessions.content:
Water Is Life – Where It Comes From and How We Use It

Water is very important. Every living thing needs water. We get water from different places.

1. Sources of Water

  • Rain: Water falls from clouds. We can collect rainwater in buckets or tanks.
  • Well: A deep hole dug into the ground where water is found.
  • Borehole: A narrow hole drilled deep, water is pumped out.
  • River or stream: Natural flowing water. Many villages get water from rivers.
  • Tap (pipe-borne water): Water that comes through pipes into our homes and schools. This is usually treated and clean.

Activity 1 – Water source walk
Walk around the school compound. Find and list all sources of water you see: a tap, a puddle, a water storage container. Discuss: Where does the water come from? (collaboration).

2. Uses of Water

  • Drinking: We need clean water to stay healthy.
  • Cooking: Water is used to cook rice, banku, soup.
  • Washing: Bathing, washing clothes, washing dishes.
  • Farming: Watering crops, giving to animals.
  • Cleaning: Mopping floors, flushing toilets.

Activity 2 – Uses of water poster
In pairs, draw a poster showing three different uses of water. Write a caption under each picture. (creativity, collaboration).

Digital corner: Watch a short video that shows the journey of water from a river to a tap. Discuss the importance of keeping rivers clean. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.2

  1. Name two sources of water found in your community.
  2. List three things you use water for at home.
  3. Why must we drink clean water? Give one reason.
  4. Draw a picture showing one way you can save water at home (e.g., turning off the tap while brushing teeth).

sessions.title: Air – Air Is All Around Us
indicators: Recognise that air exists even though we cannot see it
Demonstrate that moving air is wind (using paper, fan, or balloon)
State that all living things need air to breathe
Conduct simple experiments to show air occupies space and has force
Work in pairs to explore air with hands-on activities (collaboration)
Use digital animations to visualise air molecules (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Invisible Air – We Breathe It Every Moment

Air is all around us. We cannot see it, taste it, or smell it normally, but we can feel it and know it is there.

1. What Is Air?

Air is a mixture of gases. It fills every empty space. We breathe air in and out all the time. Without air, we would die in a few minutes.

Evidence that air exists:
– Blow air into a balloon; it inflates. The air inside takes up space.
– Wave a fan or a book near your face; you feel the moving air (wind).
– Hold a piece of paper in front of your mouth and blow; the paper moves. That is air pushing it.

Activity 1 – Feel the air
In pairs, use a straw to blow air onto your hand. Can you feel it? Then put a small piece of paper on the desk and blow it with the straw. What happens? Discuss. (collaboration).

Activity 2 – Air takes up space
Crush a piece of paper into a ball and place it at the bottom of a cup. Turn the cup upside down and push it straight down into a bowl of water. The paper stays dry! Why? Air trapped inside the cup stops water from entering. (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Watch an animation showing air particles (like tiny balls) bouncing around in a container. See how they fill the space. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.3

  1. How do you know air is around you? Give one way you can feel it.
  2. Blow up a balloon. What is inside it?
  3. Do fish need air? (Hint: They take air from water.) Write yes or no.
  4. Draw an experiment that shows air takes up space. Label it.
